lessons.title: Hash Table Concept
lessons.concept: A hash table (hash map) stores key-value pairs and uses a hash function to compute an index (bucket) from the key for fast access. On average, insertion, deletion, and lookup can be O(1), but performance depends on hash quality and collision handling.
lessons.formula: index = hash(key) mod table_size. Operations: put(key,value), get(key), delete(key).
lessons.worked_example: If hash('cat') mod 10 = 3, the pair ('cat', value) is stored in bucket 3. To look up 'cat', compute the same index and inspect bucket 3.
mistakes: Assuming hash tables always guarantee O(1) in all cases (worst case can degrade)
Forgetting that different keys can map to the same index (collision)

lessons.title: Collisions and Handling
lessons.concept: A collision occurs when two different keys produce the same bucket index. Common handling strategies include chaining (store multiple entries in a list/structure at the bucket) and open addressing (probe for another empty slot using a sequence).
lessons.formula: Chaining: bucket holds a collection of entries. Open addressing: try index, index+1, etc. according to probe scheme.
lessons.worked_example: With chaining, if keys K1 and K2 both hash to bucket 5, bucket 5 stores entries for both (e.g., a linked list). Lookup checks entries in that bucket for the matching key.
mistakes: Thinking collisions mean data is lost (proper handling preserves entries)
Confusing chaining with simply overwriting existing values
Not comparing keys during lookup in a bucket (hash match alone is not enough)

lessons.title: Use Cases and Complexity
lessons.concept: Hash tables are ideal for fast key-based lookups, counting frequencies, membership tests, and implementing maps/sets. Average-case time is O(1) for basic operations with a good hash and load factor; worst-case can be O(n) if many collisions occur. Space usage is typically O(n).
lessons.formula: Average: insert/search/delete ~ O(1). Worst: O(n) with heavy collisions. Space: O(n).
lessons.worked_example: To count word frequencies in a list, use words as keys and counts as values: for each word, update table[word] = table[word] + 1 in average O(1) per update.
mistakes: Using hash tables when ordered traversal/sorting by key is primarily required
Ignoring that poor hash functions can degrade performance
Assuming iteration order is always sorted (depends on implementation; many are unordered)

practice.question: What is the primary purpose of a hash function in a hash table?

options.B: To compute an index/bucket from a key

practice.explanation: A hash function maps a key to an index (bucket) in the hash table, enabling efficient placement and lookup.

practice.question: What is a collision in a hash table?

options.B: When two different keys map to the same index
options.C: When a key maps to index 0
options.D: When a value is deleted twice

practice.explanation: A collision occurs when the hash function produces the same bucket index for two different keys.

practice.question: Which technique handles collisions by storing multiple entries in the same bucket using a linked structure/list?
practice.explanation: Chaining resolves collisions by keeping a collection (such as a linked list) of all entries that hash to the same bucket.

practice.question: What is the average-case time complexity for lookup in a well-implemented hash table?
practice.explanation: With a good hash function and reasonable load factor, hash table lookups take average-case constant time O(1).

practice.question: Which task is a good fit for a hash table?

options.A: Finding an element by key quickly
options.B: Keeping elements in sorted order by default
options.C: Storing data only sequentially in contiguous memory
options.D: Always guaranteeing O(1) worst-case for all operations

practice.explanation: Hash tables are designed for fast key-based access (lookup/insert/delete) on average. They do not inherently maintain sorted order or guarantee worst-case O(1).

practice.question: Which collision-handling scheme stores colliding entries in a linked list (or bucket) at the same index?
practice.explanation: Separate chaining keeps a secondary structure (commonly a linked list/tree) per bucket, so multiple keys can share one index.

practice.question: In linear probing, a collision is resolved by:

options.A: Storing the key in a linked list
options.B: Placing the key in the next free slot in the table

practice.explanation: Linear probing searches forward (wrapping around) for the next empty slot - open addressing. This keeps everything in one array but can create clustering.

questions.question: During lookup in a chained hash bucket containing multiple entries, why must the key be compared?

options.A: Because bucket index alone does not guarantee key equality
options.B: To compute the hash again for sorting
options.C: Because values cannot be stored without comparison

questions.explanation: Multiple keys can hash to the same bucket (collision). After reaching the bucket, the actual key must be compared to find the correct entry.

questions.question: What is 'primary clustering' in linear probing?

options.A: Keys hashing to the first bucket only
options.B: Long runs of occupied slots that grow as more keys probe into them

questions.explanation: With linear probing, a cluster of occupied slots attracts further insertions, lengthening the run and slowing every nearby operation - motivating quadratic/double hashing.

questions.question: Why does a hash table usually rehash (resize) when the load factor gets too high?

options.B: To keep average operation time O(1) by reducing collision density
options.D: To convert to a tree automatically

questions.explanation: More entries per bucket means longer chains/probe sequences. Growing the array (typically doubling) and rehashing restores a low load factor and short chains.

questions.question: Worst-case time complexity of a hash-table lookup when every key collides into one bucket is:
questions.explanation: Degenerate hashing degrades the table to a single list scanned linearly: O(n). (Java's HashMap converts very long bins to balanced trees to soften this to O(log n).)
